CANCER AGE-CURVE SIMULATOR - BUILD SPEC (v1)
============================================
Status: DRAFT, waiting for Cameron's OK. Nothing is built yet.
Created: 2026-10-09.


GOAL
----
Answer Q1 of proposal.md: can p, which hit a carcinogen speeds up, and when
exposure starts and stops produce the downward bend at old ages in lung cancer
in men (Armitage & Doll 1954, Fig. 3; CI5 England)?

v1 does NOT answer that yet. v1 only rebuilds the Armitage & Doll straight
line (no carcinogen) and proves it is right. Everything later is built on it.


THE MODEL (v1)
--------------
1. A person is a grid of N cells (default 10 x 10 = 100). Each cell holds a
   hit count from 0 to r. Everyone starts with 0 hits in every cell.

       one person, N = 9 cells, r = 3

       +---+---+---+
       | 0 | 1 | 0 |      each number = hits that cell has so far
       +---+---+---+
       | 2 | 0 | 0 |      a cell that reaches 3 = cancer
       +---+---+---+
       | 0 | 0 | 1 |
       +---+---+---+

   In v1 the cells do not affect each other, so the grid shape does not
   matter yet. It matters later, when cells divide and have neighbors.

2. Each year of age a = 0, 1, 2, ..., 84, every cell with fewer than r hits
   gets its NEXT hit with probability p. Hits come in a fixed order: a cell
   with 1 hit can only gain hit #2, never jump to hit #3.

       one cell, r = 3, p = 0.5 (made-up coin flips):

       age:     0     1     2     3     4
       flip:   miss  HIT   miss  HIT   HIT
       hits:    0     1     1     2     3   <- cancer at age 4

3. The first year any cell reaches r hits is the person's age at cancer.
   That person stops there (they are no longer cancer-free). Nobody reaches
   r by the end of age 84 -> age at cancer = none.

4. Simulate M people (default 20,000) and store a table with one row per
   person:  { person: 0, ageAtCancer: 61 },  { person: 1, ageAtCancer: null } ...

5. Cancer rate for each five-year age group (0-4, 5-9, ..., 80-84):

       rate = (cases with ageAtCancer in the group)
              / (people still cancer-free at the start of the group x 5)

   This is cases per person-year, the same kind of number as CI5 (pop.csv
   counts person-years). See DECISION 4 for a more exact version.

6. Slope = the least-squares straight line through
   log(rate) vs log(middle age of the group), using the groups from 25-29 to
   80-84 (A&D used 25-74; CI5 goes to 85+). Groups with 0 cases are skipped,
   since log(0) does not exist.

7. Random numbers come from a seeded generator: the same seed gives the exact
   same people every time, so a test can be repeated. (JavaScript's built-in
   Math.random cannot be given a seed.)


THE EXACT ANSWER TO COMPARE AGAINST
-----------------------------------
With no carcinogen, a cell gets one yes/no chance per year, so after t years
its number of hits is min(r, Binomial(t, p)). That gives, with no simulation:

   P(one cell done by t years)  = P(Binomial(t, p) >= r)
   P(person cancer-free after t) = S(t) = (1 - P(cell done by t))^N
   expected rate in a group g..g+4 = (S(g) - S(g+5)) / (S(g) x 5)

The simulation must land close to this (HAND CHECK 6). It is a stronger check
than "slope = r - 1", which is only true when hits are rare.


FUNCTIONS (built and tested one at a time, in this order)
---------------------------------------------------------
  makeRng(seed)                    -> a function giving numbers in [0, 1)
  stepCell(hits, r, p, rand)       -> the cell's hits after one year
  simulatePerson(N, r, p, rand)    -> age at cancer, or null
  simulatePopulation(M, N, r, p, seed) -> the table of people
  ageGroupRates(table)             -> 17 groups: cases, at risk, rate
  logLogSlope(ages, rates)         -> the slope of the straight line
  expectedRates(N, r, p)           -> the exact rates from the formula above


HAND CHECKS (must pass)
-----------------------
All numbers below were worked out by hand and double-checked with a separate
calculation on 2026-10-09.

1. p = 0: nobody ever gets cancer (every ageAtCancer is null).

2. p = 1, r = 3: every cell gains a hit every year (ages 0, 1, 2), so every
   person gets cancer at age 2.

3. r = 1, N = 1 (one hit, proposal Test Case 3): the rate is flat. Each year
   the chance is p, so in every group the rate is (1 - (1 - p)^5) / 5.
   With p = 0.1: (1 - 0.59049) / 5 = 0.081902 in EVERY group.

4. logLogSlope on rates made from rate = age^3 returns exactly 3.
   Also: a flat rate (age^0) returns 0, and two points, rate 1 at age 10
   and rate 4 at age 20, return log(4) / log(2) = 2.

5. expectedRates for a tiny case, N = 1, r = 2, p = 0.5:
   - Group 0-4: after 5 coin flips, P(at least 2 heads) = 1 - 6/32 = 26/32.
     Everyone started cancer-free, so rate = (26/32) / 5 = 0.1625.
   - Group 5-9: cancer-free at 5 = 6/32 = 192/1024. Cancer-free at 10 =
     P(at most 1 head in 10) = 11/1024. Cases = 181/1024.
     Rate = (181/1024) / (192/1024) / 5 = 181/960 = 0.18854.

6. Simulation vs formula: with the default settings, each group's simulated
   case count is within 3 standard deviations (about 3 x sqrt(expected
   count)) of the expected count. See DECISION 5.

7. Slope vs r - 1 (proposal Test Cases 1 and 4): with r = 4, the slope is
   close to 3, but not equal, because hits are not perfectly rare:
     r = 4, p = 0.002 -> exact slope 2.99, but only about 56 cases in
                         20,000 people (too few to measure)
     r = 4, p = 0.005 -> exact slope 2.84, about 1,750 cases  <- default
   The simulated slope must be within 0.15 of the exact slope (2.84), and
   the gap from 3 is explained by the same flattening we measured in the
   tutor session (r = 7, p = 0.05: slopes 4.0 -> 2.6).


DEFAULTS (proposed)
-------------------
  N = 100 cells, r = 4 hits, p = 0.005 per year, M = 20,000 people, seed = 1.
  Work: 20,000 x 100 x 85 = 170 million coin flips, a second or two in node.
  Real cancers are far rarer; p is scaled up so the curve has enough cases
  (proposal Q2). Only the shape of the curve is compared with real data.

--------------------------

      Test Cases 2 (the 5,000x timing check) and 5 (the bend vs CI5) need.
  v3: the web page: sliders for p, which hit, start and stop; the log-log
      graph next to CI5 England lung cancer in men; presets.
  Later: cells that divide (Luebeck & Moolgavkar 2002), immune cells.

5. Tolerance: within 3 standard deviations for case counts, and within 0.15

content.text:
## 1) How many cells

Yes, we found three sources on Oct 7. They're in `research/cell-rules-candidates.md`:

| Source | Cells | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Luebeck & Moolgavkar 2002 | about 10^8 colon stem cells | confirmed |
| Nicholson et al. 2018 | about 10^7 crypts × about 7 stem cells per crypt ≈ 7×10^7 | confirmed |
| Tomasetti & Vogelstein 2015 | 2×10^8 | not confirmed |

All of these are about the colon. We don't have a lung number yet.

We can't simulate 10^8 cells per person, but in v1 we don't need to. When hits are rare, a person's risk by age t is about N × C(t, r) × p^r. That means N and p trade off against each other:

- **N (number of cells)** only raises or lowers the whole line. It doesn't change the slope.
- **p (chance of a hit per year)** changes the height and also controls the bend.

So 100 cells with p = 0.005 behaves almost like 10^8 cells with p = 0.005 × (100 / 10^8)^(1/4) ≈ 0.00016. We're shrinking the person for speed, and the shape of the curve stays the same.

The paper numbers start to matter in later versions. When cells sit in crypts and divide, Nicholson's 7 stem cells per crypt could set the grid layout.

## 2) Why 20,000 people

There was no real logic. I picked 20,000 as a round number that gives about 1,750 cases and should run fast. Here's a way to choose it properly.

A random count is uncertain by about √(count). For example, if 100 cases are expected, you'll usually get 90–110 (±10%).

The fewest cases come in the youngest group we fit, ages 25–29:

| People | Expected cases at 25–29 | Noise |
|---|---|---|
| 20,000 | about 16 | √16 = 4, so ±25% |
| about 123,000 | 100 | ±10% |

**Rule:** pick the smallest number of people that gives at least 100 expected cases in the 25–29 group. The catch is speed: 123,000 people is about 6× the work. We'll time it when we build `simulatePopulation`. Keeping 20,000 for now is fine.

## 3) Why r = 4 and p = 0.005

**r = 4:** I picked it for the math check, not for biology. Slope 3 is easy to recognize, and a small r runs fast. There are real-data choices for later:
- Armitage & Doll's Table I slopes are 5–6.5, so r = 6–7.
- CI5 England lung cancer in men has a slope of about 8, so r ≈ 9.

**p = 0.005:** this one has some logic, as a trade-off.
- A smaller p gives a slope closer to r − 1 but fewer cases. At p = 0.002 the slope is 2.99, but there are only about 56 cases.
- A larger p gives more cases but more bending. At p = 0.005 there are about 1,750 cases, with a slope of 2.84.

The bend grows with p × age, so a rule could be "the largest p that keeps the exact slope within 0.2 of r − 1." Whatever we pick, the exact formula tells us the right slope.

## 4) The rate formula

The rate means **cases per year spent at risk**. The question is how to count those years. Take the age 60–64 group with 1,000 cancer-free people at age 60, where 50 get cancer during the group:

- **Simple:** assume everyone was at risk all 5 years. That's 1,000 × 5 = 5,000 person-years, so the rate is 50 / 5,000 = 0.0100.
- **Exact person-years:** someone who got cancer at 61 was only at risk for 2 of those years (60 and 61). If the 50 cases average 3 years each, that's 950 × 5 + 50 × 3 = 4,900 person-years, so the rate is 50 / 4,900 = 0.0102.

When cancer is rare, the two barely differ. When it's common, they do. In hand check 3 (one hit, p = 0.1):
- simple gives 0.0819;
- exact person-years gives exactly 0.1000, which is p itself.

The exact count is cleaner and closer to how CI5 counts, so I'd lean that way. Hand check 3 would then become "rate = p".

## 5) The tolerance

The simulation is random, so it never matches the formula exactly. The tolerance is how far off counts as "still correct" before the test fails.

- **3 standard deviations:** if 100 cases are expected, the standard deviation is about √100 = 10, so 70–130 passes. A correct program lands inside this range 99.7% of the time. The cost is that a bug that's off by only 20% could still slip through, so a stricter check (for example ±2.5 standard deviations) is an option.
- **0.15 on the slope:** this was a guess. To set it properly, run the simulation with about 20 different seeds, see how much the slope varies from run to run, and set the tolerance to about 3× that spread.

To redo the spec with these choices, I need two answers from you:
- Exact person-years, or the simple count?
- Should the spec say how we'll pick the number of people and the slope tolerance by measuring them, rather than using fixed guesses?

CANCER AGE-CURVE SIMULATOR - BUILD SPEC (v1)
============================================
Status: DRAFT, waiting for Cameron's OK. Nothing is built yet.
Created: 2026-10-09.


GOAL
----
Answer Q1 of proposal.md: can p, which hit a carcinogen speeds up, and when
exposure starts and stops produce the downward bend at old ages in lung cancer
in men (Armitage & Doll 1954, Fig. 3; CI5 England)?

v1 does NOT answer that yet. v1 only rebuilds the Armitage & Doll straight
line (no carcinogen) and proves it is right. Everything later is built on it.


THE MODEL (v1)
--------------
1. A person is a grid of N cells (default 10 x 10 = 100). Each cell holds a
   hit count from 0 to r. Everyone starts with 0 hits in every cell.

       one person, N = 9 cells, r = 3

       +---+---+---+
       | 0 | 1 | 0 |      each number = hits that cell has so far
       +---+---+---+
       | 2 | 0 | 0 |      a cell that reaches 3 = cancer
       +---+---+---+
       | 0 | 0 | 1 |
       +---+---+---+

   In v1 the cells do not affect each other, so the grid shape does not
   matter yet. It matters later, when cells divide and have neighbors.

2. Each year of age a = 0, 1, 2, ..., 84, every cell with fewer than r hits
   gets its NEXT hit with probability p. Hits come in a fixed order: a cell
   with 1 hit can only gain hit #2, never jump to hit #3.

       one cell, r = 3, p = 0.5 (made-up coin flips):

       age:     0     1     2     3     4
       flip:   miss  HIT   miss  HIT   HIT
       hits:    0     1     1     2     3   <- cancer at age 4

3. The first year any cell reaches r hits is the person's age at cancer.
   That person stops there (they are no longer cancer-free). Nobody reaches
   r by the end of age 84 -> age at cancer = none.

4. Simulate M people (default 20,000) and store a table with one row per
   person:  { person: 0, ageAtCancer: 61 },  { person: 1, ageAtCancer: null } ...

5. Cancer rate for each five-year age group (0-4, 5-9, ..., 80-84):

       rate = (cases with ageAtCancer in the group)
              / (people still cancer-free at the start of the group x 5)

   This is cases per person-year, the same kind of number as CI5 (pop.csv
   counts person-years). See DECISION 4 for a more exact version.

6. Slope = the least-squares straight line through
   log(rate) vs log(middle age of the group), using the groups from 25-29 to
   80-84 (A&D used 25-74; CI5 goes to 85+). Groups with 0 cases are skipped,
   since log(0) does not exist.

7. Random numbers come from a seeded generator: the same seed gives the exact
   same people every time, so a test can be repeated. (JavaScript's built-in
   Math.random cannot be given a seed.)


THE EXACT ANSWER TO COMPARE AGAINST
-----------------------------------
With no carcinogen, a cell gets one yes/no chance per year, so after t years
its number of hits is min(r, Binomial(t, p)). That gives, with no simulation:

   P(one cell done by t years)  = P(Binomial(t, p) >= r)
   P(person cancer-free after t) = S(t) = (1 - P(cell done by t))^N
   expected rate in a group g..g+4 = (S(g) - S(g+5)) / (S(g) x 5)

The simulation must land close to this (HAND CHECK 6). It is a stronger check
than "slope = r - 1", which is only true when hits are rare.


FUNCTIONS (built and tested one at a time, in this order)
---------------------------------------------------------
  makeRng(seed)                    -> a function giving numbers in [0, 1)
  stepCell(hits, r, p, rand)       -> the cell's hits after one year
  simulatePerson(N, r, p, rand)    -> age at cancer, or null
  simulatePopulation(M, N, r, p, seed) -> the table of people
  ageGroupRates(table)             -> 17 groups: cases, at risk, rate
  logLogSlope(ages, rates)         -> the slope of the straight line
  expectedRates(N, r, p)           -> the exact rates from the formula above


HAND CHECKS (must pass)
-----------------------
All numbers below were worked out by hand and double-checked with a separate
calculation on 2026-10-09.

1. p = 0: nobody ever gets cancer (every ageAtCancer is null).

2. p = 1, r = 3: every cell gains a hit every year (ages 0, 1, 2), so every
   person gets cancer at age 2.

3. r = 1, N = 1 (one hit, proposal Test Case 3): the rate is flat. Each year
   the chance is p, so in every group the rate is (1 - (1 - p)^5) / 5.
   With p = 0.1: (1 - 0.59049) / 5 = 0.081902 in EVERY group.

4. logLogSlope on rates made from rate = age^3 returns exactly 3.
   Also: a flat rate (age^0) returns 0, and two points, rate 1 at age 10
   and rate 4 at age 20, return log(4) / log(2) = 2.

5. expectedRates for a tiny case, N = 1, r = 2, p = 0.5:
   - Group 0-4: after 5 coin flips, P(at least 2 heads) = 1 - 6/32 = 26/32.
     Everyone started cancer-free, so rate = (26/32) / 5 = 0.1625.
   - Group 5-9: cancer-free at 5 = 6/32 = 192/1024. Cancer-free at 10 =
     P(at most 1 head in 10) = 11/1024. Cases = 181/1024.
     Rate = (181/1024) / (192/1024) / 5 = 181/960 = 0.18854.

6. Simulation vs formula: with the default settings, each group's simulated
   case count is within 3 standard deviations (about 3 x sqrt(expected
   count)) of the expected count. See DECISION 5.

7. Slope vs r - 1 (proposal Test Cases 1 and 4): with r = 4, the slope is
   close to 3, but not equal, because hits are not perfectly rare:
     r = 4, p = 0.002 -> exact slope 2.99, but only about 56 cases in
                         20,000 people (too few to measure)
     r = 4, p = 0.005 -> exact slope 2.84, about 1,750 cases  <- default
   The simulated slope must be within 0.15 of the exact slope (2.84), and
   the gap from 3 is explained by the same flattening we measured in the
   tutor session (r = 7, p = 0.05: slopes 4.0 -> 2.6).


DEFAULTS (proposed)
-------------------
  N = 100 cells, r = 4 hits, p = 0.005 per year, M = 20,000 people, seed = 1.
  Work: 20,000 x 100 x 85 = up to 170 million coin flips per run. Not timed
  yet; we measure it when simulatePopulation is built.
  Real cancers are far rarer; p is scaled up so the curve has enough cases
  (proposal Q2). Only the shape of the curve is compared with real data.


NOT IN v1 (later versions)
--------------------------
  v2: the carcinogen. It multiplies p for ONE chosen hit (#1 ... #r) between a
      start age and a stop age. This is what Q1 asks about, and what proposal
      Test Cases 2 (the 5,000x timing check) and 5 (the bend vs CI5) need.
  v3: the web page: sliders for p, which hit, start and stop; the log-log
      graph next to CI5 England lung cancer in men; presets.
  Later: cells that divide (Luebeck & Moolgavkar 2002), immune cells.


DECISIONS FOR CAMERON (OK the default, or change it)
----------------------------------------------------
1. Cells per person N: 100 (10 x 10)?
2. People M: 20,000?
3. Default r = 4 and p = 0.005 for the v1 checks? (A&D's real sites need
   r of about 6-7; lung in CI5 England looks like 9. Those come in v2 with
   a scaled-up p.)
4. Rate formula: "cancer-free at start of group x 5" (simple, matches the
   hand checks above) or exact person-years (count each person's years
   cancer-free inside the group; closer to how CI5 counts)?
5. Tolerance: within 3 standard deviations for case counts, and within 0.15
   for the slope?

Status: DRAFT, waiting for Cameron's OK. Nothing is built yet.

----
Answer Q1 of proposal.md: can p, which hit a carcinogen speeds up, and when
exposure starts and stops produce the downward bend at old ages in lung cancer
in men (Armitage & Doll 1954, Fig. 3; CI5 England)?

v1 does NOT answer that yet. v1 only rebuilds the Armitage & Doll straight
line (no carcinogen) and proves it is right. Everything later is built on it.

1. A person is a grid of N cells (default 10 x 10 = 100). Each cell holds a
   hit count from 0 to r. Everyone starts with 0 hits in every cell.

       one person, N = 9 cells, r = 3

       +---+---+---+
       | 0 | 1 | 0 |      each number = hits that cell has so far
       +---+---+---+
       | 2 | 0 | 0 |      a cell that reaches 3 = cancer
       +---+---+---+
       | 0 | 0 | 1 |
       +---+---+---+

   In v1 the cells do not affect each other, so the grid shape does not
   matter yet. It matters later, when cells divide and have neighbors.

2. Each year of age a = 0, 1, 2, ..., 84, every cell with fewer than r hits
   gets its NEXT hit with probability p. Hits come in a fixed order: a cell
   with 1 hit can only gain hit #2, never jump to hit #3.

       one cell, r = 3, p = 0.5 (made-up coin flips):

       age:     0     1     2     3     4
       flip:   miss  HIT   miss  HIT   HIT
       hits:    0     1     1     2     3   <- cancer at age 4

3. The first year any cell reaches r hits is the person's age at cancer.
   That person stops there (they are no longer cancer-free). Nobody reaches
   r by the end of age 84 -> age at cancer = none.

4. Simulate M people (default 20,000) and store a table with one row per
   person:  { person: 0, ageAtCancer: 61 },  { person: 1, ageAtCancer: null } ...

5. Cancer rate for each five-year age group (0-4, 5-9, ..., 80-84), using
   exact person-years (decided 2026-10-09):

       rate = (cases with ageAtCancer in the group)
              / (person-years at risk in the group)

   A person adds 1 person-year for each year of age in the group that they
   START cancer-free, including the year they get cancer. Example, group
   60-64: cancer-free all 5 years -> 5; cancer at 61 -> 2 (ages 60 and 61);
   cancer before 60 -> 0.
   This is cases per person-year, like CI5 (pop.csv counts person-years).
   (CI5 divides by everyone alive, including people who already had cancer;
   for a rare cancer the difference is tiny.)

   log(rate) vs log(middle age of the group), using the groups from 25-29 to

   (top: share of people who get cancer in the group; bottom: expected
   person-years at risk, one year for each age they start cancer-free)

than "slope = r - 1", which is only true when hits are rare.

content.text:
I updated `spec.txt` for points 2 and 4:
- **People:** 20,000 now and about 100,000 later, with the rule for choosing the number.
- **Rate:** exact person-years.
- **Hand checks:** two changed with the new rate formula.
  - Check 3: one hit now gives a rate of exactly p in every group.
  - Check 5: the coin-flip case now gives 13/57 = 0.228. I worked it out by hand and it matches the separate script.

Your other three questions are answered below.

## 1) A correction first

You're close, but two pieces are mixed up:
- **N is cells per person**, not people. The trade-off is between the number of cells in each person and p.
- **p^r is p to the power of the number of hits**, not years. The formula reads: (number of cells) × (ways to fit r hits into t years) × p^r.

So "fewer cells, larger p" keeps the same curve. The number of people is separate. It only controls how noisy the curve is.

### On realism

That's a reasonable priority, and it leads to a real scientific finding. Let's plug in real numbers:
- about 10^8 cells (Luebeck & Moolgavkar 2002);
- a real per-cell mutation rate of about 1.4×10⁻⁶ per year (their Table 1, for the APC gene);
- r = 6, up to age 70.

The chance of cancer by age 70 is about 10⁻¹⁹. Even with 100,000 people, nobody would get cancer.

This isn't a bug in our numbers. It's a known weakness of the pure Armitage & Doll model: with independent cells and real mutation rates, 6–7 hits almost never happen. It's why Moolgavkar & Knudson (1981) and Luebeck & Moolgavkar (2002) added **cells that divide**. A cell with one hit grows into a clone, so the later hits have many more chances. With that change, 4 hits and real mutation rates fit real colon data.

There's also a practical point. 10^8 cells is too many to flip one by one. But in v1 the cells are independent, so we could track only how many cells have 0, 1, 2… hits. That makes real cell counts possible.

So there are two honest options:
- **(a)** v1 keeps a scaled-up p, clearly labeled as a stand-in that only reproduces the shape. Realism comes in the next version with dividing cells, using Luebeck's real numbers.
- **(b)** Same as (a), plus one "real numbers" run in v1 that shows the pure model gives essentially no cancer. That gap becomes a finding for your discussion section and the reason for adding dividing cells.

Both are your call. Either way, it changes the project's direction, so we should check it against `course/guidelines.md` together.

## 3) What p is

- **In biology,** p is the chance per year that one cell gets the specific mutation for its next hit. It's roughly a mutation rate per cell per year, and real values are around 10⁻⁶.
- **In the paper,** Armitage & Doll never give p. They only use the slope, which depends on r and not on p. We wrote that down in `papers/armitage-doll-1954-notes.md` under "what the paper doesn't give".
- **The end goal** isn't to find "the correct p." Q1 asks what happens when p for one hit changes during life (exposure starting and stopping). So p is a dial we turn, not an answer we're looking for.
- **If we did fit p** to CI5, the pure model would need a p far above the real mutation rate. That gap is the finding from point 1.

## 4) Done

One small precision: CI5 divides by everyone alive, including people who already had cancer, while we divide by cancer-free people. For a rare cancer the difference is tiny, and the spec notes it.

## 5) R²: yes to a score for every run, but not R² alone

R² measures **how straight** the points are, not **whether the slope is right**. Suppose a bug made every rate grow like age² when it should grow like age³. The points would sit exactly on a line with slope 2, so R² = 1.00, a "perfect" score, even though the answer should be 3.

So I'd report several numbers for every run:
- **the slope**, compared with the exact slope (2.84);
- **R² of the line**, which says how straight the curve is. This will be useful later, because the bend should lower it.
- **the gap between the simulation and the formula** in each age group, measured in standard deviations.

The automated tests still need a pass/fail line. We can set that line by running about 20 seeds and seeing how much the numbers vary from run to run.

What I need from you: option (a) or (b) for point 1, and whether the three numbers per run in point 5 work for you.

CANCER AGE-CURVE SIMULATOR - BUILD SPEC (v1)
============================================
Status: DRAFT, waiting for Cameron's OK. Nothing is built yet.
Created: 2026-10-09.


GOAL
----
Answer Q1 of proposal.md: can p, which hit a carcinogen speeds up, and when
exposure starts and stops produce the downward bend at old ages in lung cancer
in men (Armitage & Doll 1954, Fig. 3; CI5 England)?

v1 does NOT answer that yet. v1 only rebuilds the Armitage & Doll straight
line (no carcinogen) and proves it is right. Everything later is built on it.


THE MODEL (v1)
--------------
1. A person is a grid of N cells (default 10 x 10 = 100). Each cell holds a
   hit count from 0 to r. Everyone starts with 0 hits in every cell.

       one person, N = 9 cells, r = 3

       +---+---+---+
       | 0 | 1 | 0 |      each number = hits that cell has so far
       +---+---+---+
       | 2 | 0 | 0 |      a cell that reaches 3 = cancer
       +---+---+---+
       | 0 | 0 | 1 |
       +---+---+---+

   In v1 the cells do not affect each other, so the grid shape does not
   matter yet. It matters later, when cells divide and have neighbors.

2. Each year of age a = 0, 1, 2, ..., 84, every cell with fewer than r hits
   gets its NEXT hit with probability p. Hits come in a fixed order: a cell
   with 1 hit can only gain hit #2, never jump to hit #3.

       one cell, r = 3, p = 0.5 (made-up coin flips):

       age:     0     1     2     3     4
       flip:   miss  HIT   miss  HIT   HIT
       hits:    0     1     1     2     3   <- cancer at age 4

3. The first year any cell reaches r hits is the person's age at cancer.
   That person stops there (they are no longer cancer-free). Nobody reaches
   r by the end of age 84 -> age at cancer = none.

4. Simulate M people (default 20,000) and store a table with one row per
   person:  { person: 0, ageAtCancer: 61 },  { person: 1, ageAtCancer: null } ...

5. Cancer rate for each five-year age group (0-4, 5-9, ..., 80-84), using
   exact person-years (decided 2026-10-09):

       rate = (cases with ageAtCancer in the group)
              / (person-years at risk in the group)

   A person adds 1 person-year for each year of age in the group that they
   START cancer-free, including the year they get cancer. Example, group
   60-64: cancer-free all 5 years -> 5; cancer at 61 -> 2 (ages 60 and 61);
   cancer before 60 -> 0.
   This is cases per person-year, like CI5 (pop.csv counts person-years).
   (CI5 divides by everyone alive, including people who already had cancer;
   for a rare cancer the difference is tiny.)

6. Slope = the least-squares straight line through
   log(rate) vs log(middle age of the group), using the groups from 25-29 to
   80-84 (A&D used 25-74; CI5 goes to 85+). Groups with 0 cases are skipped,
   since log(0) does not exist.

7. Random numbers come from a seeded generator: the same seed gives the exact
   same people every time, so a test can be repeated. (JavaScript's built-in
   Math.random cannot be given a seed.)


THE EXACT ANSWER TO COMPARE AGAINST
-----------------------------------
With no carcinogen, a cell gets one yes/no chance per year, so after t years
its number of hits is min(r, Binomial(t, p)). That gives, with no simulation:

   P(one cell done by t years)  = P(Binomial(t, p) >= r)
   P(person cancer-free after t) = S(t) = (1 - P(cell done by t))^N
   expected rate in a group g..g+4 =
       (S(g) - S(g+5)) / (S(g) + S(g+1) + S(g+2) + S(g+3) + S(g+4))
   (top: share of people who get cancer in the group; bottom: expected
   person-years at risk, one year for each age they start cancer-free)

The simulation must land close to this (HAND CHECK 6). It is a stronger check
than "slope = r - 1", which is only true when hits are rare.


FUNCTIONS (built and tested one at a time, in this order)
---------------------------------------------------------
  makeRng(seed)                    -> a function giving numbers in [0, 1)
  stepCell(hits, r, p, rand)       -> the cell's hits after one year
  simulatePerson(N, r, p, rand)    -> age at cancer, or null
  simulatePopulation(M, N, r, p, seed) -> the table of people
  ageGroupRates(table)             -> 17 groups: cases, at risk, rate
  logLogSlope(ages, rates)         -> the slope of the straight line
  expectedRates(N, r, p)           -> the exact rates from the formula above


HAND CHECKS (must pass)
-----------------------
All numbers below were worked out by hand and double-checked with a separate
calculation on 2026-10-09.

1. p = 0: nobody ever gets cancer (every ageAtCancer is null).

2. p = 1, r = 3: every cell gains a hit every year (ages 0, 1, 2), so every
   person gets cancer at age 2.

3. r = 1, N = 1 (one hit, proposal Test Case 3): the rate is flat. Each year
   a cancer-free person has chance p, so cases per person-year = p exactly.
   With p = 0.1: expectedRates gives 0.1 in EVERY group.

4. logLogSlope on rates made from rate = age^3 returns exactly 3.
   Also: a flat rate (age^0) returns 0, and two points, rate 1 at age 10
   and rate 4 at age 20, return log(4) / log(2) = 2.

5. expectedRates for a tiny case, N = 1, r = 2, p = 0.5 (a coin flip each
   year; cancer = the 2nd head). S(a) = P(at most 1 head in a flips):
     S(0) = 1, S(1) = 1, S(2) = 3/4, S(3) = 4/8 = 1/2, S(4) = 5/16,
     S(5) = 6/32 = 3/16.
   - Group 0-4: cases = 1 - 3/16 = 13/16.
     Person-years = 1 + 1 + 3/4 + 1/2 + 5/16 = 57/16.
     Rate = 13/57 = 0.22807.
   - Group 5-9 (needs S(5) ... S(10) = 11/1024): rate = 181/424 = 0.42689.

6. Simulation vs formula: with the default settings, each group's simulated
   case count is within 3 standard deviations (about 3 x sqrt(expected
   count)) of the expected count. See DECISION 5.

7. Slope vs r - 1 (proposal Test Cases 1 and 4): with r = 4, the slope is
   close to 3, but not equal, because hits are not perfectly rare:
     r = 4, p = 0.002 -> exact slope 2.99, but only about 56 cases in
                         20,000 people (too few to measure)
     r = 4, p = 0.005 -> exact slope 2.84, about 1,750 cases  <- default
   The simulated slope must be within 0.15 of the exact slope (2.84), and
   the gap from 3 is explained by the same flattening we measured in the
   tutor session (r = 7, p = 0.05: slopes 4.0 -> 2.6).


DEFAULTS (proposed)
-------------------
  N = 100 cells, r = 4 hits, p = 0.005 per year, seed = 1.
  M = 20,000 people for now (decided 2026-10-09); about 100,000 for the
  final versions. Rule for choosing M later: enough people that the 25-29
  group expects at least 100 cases (noise about +-10%), if it runs fast enough.
  Work: 20,000 x 100 x 85 = up to 170 million coin flips per run. Not timed
  yet; we measure it when simulatePopulation is built.
  Real cancers are far rarer; p is scaled up so the curve has enough cases
  (proposal Q2). Only the shape of the curve is compared with real data.


NOT IN v1 (later versions)
--------------------------
  v2: the carcinogen. It multiplies p for ONE chosen hit (#1 ... #r) between a
      start age and a stop age. This is what Q1 asks about, and what proposal
      Test Cases 2 (the 5,000x timing check) and 5 (the bend vs CI5) need.
  v3: the web page: sliders for p, which hit, start and stop; the log-log
      graph next to CI5 England lung cancer in men; presets.
  Later: cells that divide (Luebeck & Moolgavkar 2002), immune cells.


DECISIONS FOR CAMERON (OK the default, or change it)
----------------------------------------------------
1. Cells per person N: 100 (10 x 10)?
2. People M: DECIDED, 20,000 now, about 100,000 later.
3. Default r = 4 and p = 0.005 for the v1 checks? (A&D's real sites need
   r of about 6-7; lung in CI5 England looks like 9.) Open: Cameron wants the
   model rooted in real numbers (discussion 2026-10-09).
4. Rate formula: DECIDED, exact person-years.
5. Tolerance: open. Cameron suggested reporting a score per run (R squared)
   instead of only pass/fail (discussion 2026-10-09).

lines: same people every time, so a test can be repeated. (JavaScript's built-in
Math.random cannot be given a seed.)

+     straight). It does NOT say the slope is right: rates growing like age^2

+   - a z-score for each age group: how far the simulated case count is from

+         z = (simulated cases - expected cases) / sqrt(expected cases)

`spec.txt` now has all five decisions settled. It's ready for a final read before we build anything. Here's what changed for option (b) and the three numbers:

- **Three numbers per run:** every run reports the slope (shown next to the exact slope), R² of the line, and a z-score for each age group. The spec notes that R² alone can't catch a wrong slope.
- **Pass lines:** these will be measured, not guessed. We run 20 seeds, see how much the numbers vary from run to run, and set the pass line at about 3× that variation.
- **New hand checks:**
  - Line fitting on the points (0,0), (1,2), (2,1), done by hand: slope 0.5, R² = 0.25.
  - z-scores: 100 cases expected and 130 simulated gives z = 3.
  - **Check 8, real numbers:** the risk comes from the formula, not the simulation. Simulating 10^8 cells one at a time is too slow, and it could only ever show 0 cases. With 10^8 cells and p = 1.4×10⁻⁶ per year, lifetime risk is about 0.5 for 2 hits, 7.8×10⁻¹⁰ for 4 hits, and 3.3×10⁻¹⁹ for 6 hits.
- **A computer-arithmetic trap,** which I found while checking:
  - The obvious way to compute the 6-hit number, "1 − P(fewer than 6 hits)", gives 3.3×10⁻¹⁵ when the real answer is 3.29×10⁻²⁷. A computer only keeps about 16 digits, so subtracting from a number extremely close to 1 loses the answer.
  - The spec says to add up the exact terms directly and to use `Math.log1p` / `Math.expm1`. Check 8 tests this.
- **`progress-log.md`:** has a section for these decisions.

Changed files, ready for you to stage and commit in your own words: `CLAUDE.md`, `spec.txt`, `progress-log.md`.

Once you've read the spec and are happy with it, the first thing to build is `makeRng`, the seeded random-number generator. We'll do it as one function with its tests, and you'll run them yourself.

# 02-120 final project: a cancer model — working with Cameron

## Who I am

- Cameron, an undergraduate at Carnegie Mellon taking 02-120 Programming for
  Scientists (Python).
- This is my final project. I'm building it with Claude while still understanding
  every line that ends up in it. My last project of this kind was a simulator of
  Nowak & May (1992), "Evolutionary games and spatial chaos", deployed as a teaching
  web page (https://spatial-game.vercel.app/). This one does the same for cancer,
  starting from Hanahan's "Hallmarks of cancer" (Cell, 2026 version).
- `progress-log.md` says where the project stands. Read its latest entry first in
  a new session, and add an entry at the end of each session.
- Background from before this repo existed: `cancer-project-handoff/HANDOFF.md`
  (local only, not committed).

## How I like to work

- **One idea at a time.** Introduce a single concept, function or change, make sure
  I understand it, then move on. Don't bundle several new ideas into one step.
- **Never hand me code I can't verify.** Every piece of code comes with a way for
  me to check it myself:
  - a plain-English explanation of what it does and why,
  - tests that define what "correct" means, including edge cases (use the
    `test-every-function` skill),
  - and the command to run them, with the output shown.
  Explain checks with numbers I can verify by hand, not by reading code back to me.
  If I couldn't explain it back or check it on my own, it's too big a step.
- **Show me pictures.** Draw small images of test cases and simulation steps so I
  can see what a check means.
- **Small, runnable steps.** Each step should leave the program in a state that
  runs, so I can see the effect of the change on its own.
- **Spec first.** Write the plan into `spec.txt` and get my OK before building.
- **Ask before assuming.** If a design choice is mine to make, ask me rather than
  picking silently.
- **Learning over speed.** When I'm learning a new concept, teach it one piece at
  a time and check my understanding (the `learn-with-ai-tutor` skill) instead of
  giving me the finished answer.
- **Check against the source.** Verify model rules and numbers against the paper
  itself. Say so plainly when something was misread.

## Graded work

- Keep checking the project idea against the course project guidelines
  (`course/guidelines.md`, summarizing `course/Project Description F26.pdf`),
  especially when the concept changes. `concept.md` is a working draft and its
  guideline check table should stay current.
- The project must answer a scientific question. A game alone is explicitly not
  accepted; any game layer must serve the question.
- I write commit messages myself, in my own words. Stage changes and suggest
  what changed, but let me write the message.

The proposal and project are graded. Help me think, explain, and quiz me, but the
proposal answers are written in my words.

## Code conventions

- Use whatever language fits the project's goals best (decided 2026-10-09). The
  app must run on the web with nothing to install, so this project uses
  JavaScript, with no build step and no libraries for the model.
- Plain functions, with a short `/** ... */` comment on each.
- Model logic lives in `web/model.js`, separate from drawing and buttons
  (`web/app.js`, `web/index.html`).
- Tests live in `web/model.test.js` and run with `node model.test.js` from `web/`.
  They use the same `check` / `checkClose` / `checkThrows` helpers as the
  spatial-games project. Expected numbers are worked out by hand, not copied
  from the program's output.

# Test every function

## What this skill does
It flips the AI from "make it run" to "prove it is right." When it is on, the AI does not consider a function done until it has said what success means, written tests that cover the ordinary case and the edges, and shown you the tests so you can judge them. You stay the manager who owns "done."

## The rule you are enforcing
Karpathy's line: today's AI automates what you can **verify**. So the skill is not writing tests by hand, it is telling the AI what counts as success and demanding every function be tested against it. The bar for every function: **would you bet a million dollars this is right?** If not, it is not tested enough.

## How to respond when this skill is active
1. **Specify success first.** Before testing a function, state in one plain sentence what it must do and how you will know it worked. If the spec is vague, ask the user to sharpen it. A vague ask gets a confident wrong answer.
2. **Test every function on its own.** Break the work into small functions and check each one. Checking that the whole program runs is not the same as checking each piece is correct.
3. **Hit the edges as well as the happy path.** For each function, enumerate: the ordinary case, the empty/zero/one case, the boundary case, and the case the spec is silent on. Write a test for each.
4. **Name the silent-failure trap.** A function that returns a hardcoded answer for the one input you tested will pass that test and still be wrong. So test more than one input, and test inputs whose answer you can compute independently.
5. **Show the tests and the reasoning.** Print the tests and say what each one is checking, so the human can confirm the coverage. Do not hide verification inside "looks good."
6. **Verify without a human where you can.** Prefer checks the code can run itself (assert expected == actual) over "eyeball the output." If a check truly needs human judgment, say so and keep the human in the loop for that one.
7. **Report honestly.** End with: which functions are covered, which edges are tested, and where you would NOT yet bet $1M. Do not declare done past that line.

## Good practice
- Plan top-down, test bottom-up: design the whole thing first, then verify the small pieces that make it up.
- One behavior per test, with a name that says what it checks.
- When a test fails, fix the code or the spec, then re-run; never delete a failing test to make it green.
- Testing is a craft. The goal is coverage of the ways this specific function can go wrong, rather than a fixed number of tests.

## Pitfalls
- Tests that only re-run the happy path give false confidence.
- Asserting on output you never independently computed just checks the code agrees with itself.
- "It compiles and runs" is the black-box gambler's standard. The manager's standard is "I can show you why it is right."
I'll start with the first function from the spec, `makeRng`, and stop after it so you can check it before we move on.

content.text: Next, a check that the generator really is mulberry32. I wrote it again separately in Python with plain arithmetic in place of JavaScript's bit tricks, to get the first few numbers for seed 1:

input.command:
python3 - <<'EOF'
M = 2**32
def mul(a, b): return (a * b) % M          # 32-bit multiply, like Math.imul (mod 2^32)
def mulberry32(seed):
    state = seed
    while True:
        state = (state + 0x6D2B79F5) % M
        t = state
        t = mul(t ^ (t >> 15), t | 1)
        t = t ^ ((t + mul(t ^ (t >> 7), t | 61)) % M)
        yield (t ^ (t >> 14)) / M
for seed in (1, 0, 42):
    g = mulberry32(seed); print(seed, [next(g) for _ in range(3)])
EOF

`makeRng`, the seeded random-number generator, is built in `web/model.js`, and all 20 of its tests pass. I stopped there so you can check it before we build `stepCell`.

To run the tests yourself:

```
! cd web && node model.test.js
```

You should see `20 passed, 0 failed`.

**What the tests check:**

| # | Check | How you can verify it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | It really is mulberry32 | The first numbers match a version I wrote separately in Python (seeds 1, 0 and 42) |
| 2–4 | The same seed gives the same sequence, different seeds differ, and two generators don't interfere | Compared directly |
| 5 | Every number is in [0, 1) | Counted over 10,000 draws |
| 6 | Evenly spread | Below 0.3: expect 3,000 of 10,000, sd = √(10000 × 0.3 × 0.7) = 45.8, so 2,863–3,137 passes. Got **3,025**. |
| 7 | Neighboring numbers unrelated | Both in a pair below 0.5: expect ¼ of 5,000 = 1,250, sd 30.6, so 1,158–1,342 passes. Got **1,246**. |
| 8–9 | Edge seeds (0 and 4,294,967,295) work; bad seeds (1.5, −1, too big, text, missing) are refused | Run directly |

**Proof the tests can fail:** I ran them on two deliberately broken copies, in memory only. The file wasn't changed.
- **Bit-scrambling step removed: 6 tests fail.** Seeds 0, 1 and 42 all started near 0.4264, so the outputs follow each other. The pair test caught it: only 369 pairs fell below 0.5 instead of about 1,250.
- **Seed check removed: 3 tests fail.** A seed of 1.5 was quietly accepted.

**Where I would not yet bet $1M:**
- The bit-scrambling lines match a version I wrote separately in Python, but only for 5 numbers.
- The evenness tests catch big problems, not subtle ones. mulberry32 is a well-known generator, and that's fine for coin flips. It isn't good enough for cryptography, which we don't need.
- Each spread test uses one seed, so a correct generator could fail one by bad luck about 0.3% of the time. Because the seeds are fixed, a passing test always passes.

**A question for you** before we move on: why does test 1 use three different seeds rather than only seed 1? Think about what a lazy or wrong `makeRng` could do to still pass a single-seed test.

New and changed files, ready for you to commit in your own words: `web/model.js`, `web/model.test.js`, plus the earlier `CLAUDE.md`, `spec.txt` and `progress-log.md`. The `journal/` files changed too, because the hook updates them on its own.

content.text:
Yes. A version that always returned 0.627… would pass a seed-1-only test, and so would one that ignored the seed completely. Checking seeds 0 and 42 as well makes both of those fail. You saw this in the broken copy without bit scrambling: all three seeds started near 0.4264, which gave it away.

Next is **`stepCell`**, one year for one cell.

**Success in one sentence:** given a cell's hit count, it returns the count after one year: +1 with chance p if the cell has fewer than r hits, otherwise unchanged. It never jumps by 2, and never goes past r.

**How "with chance p" works:** draw a number from `rand()`. If it is below p, the cell gets a hit. The numbers are spread evenly over [0, 1), so landing in [0, p) happens a fraction p of the time.

```
0 ─────── p ─────────────────── 1
[  hit   )[        miss         )
```

**Two deliberately broken copies, to make sure the tests can fail:**

content.text:
That's right. The person escapes cancer at age 0 only if all 10 cells miss, which has chance 0.9¹⁰ = 0.349. So the chance of cancer is 1 − 0.349 = 0.651.

Adding 10 × 10% double-counts the people where two or more cells hit in the same year. That's why the sum can reach 100%, or go past it with 11 cells, which can't be right for a probability. For small chances the two answers nearly agree: 10 cells at p = 0.001 gives 1 − 0.999¹⁰ = 0.00996, compared with 10 × 0.001 = 0.01. This is the same reason the spec's formula is (1 − P)ᴺ and not N × P.

+ * Cancer rate for each five-year age group 0-4, 5-9, ..., 80-84 (17 groups),
+ * using exact person-years (spec.txt, MODEL item 5).
+ * A person adds 1 person-year for each age in the group that they START

+function ageGroupRates(table) {
+  const groups = [];
+  for (let start = 0; start < YEARS; start += 5) {
+    const end = start + 4;
+    let cases = 0;
+    let personYears = 0;
+    for (const row of table) {
+      // The last age this person was at risk: their cancer age, or 84 if none.
+      const lastAge = row.ageAtCancer === null ? YEARS - 1 : row.ageAtCancer;
+      personYears += Math.max(0, Math.min(lastAge, end) - start + 1);
+      if (row.ageAtCancer !== null && row.ageAtCancer >= start && row.ageAtCancer <= end) cases++;
+    groups.push({ start, end, cases, personYears, rate: personYears > 0 ? cases / personYears : null });

Base directory for this skill: /private/tmp/claude-502/bundled-skills/2.1.295/d1968f2f1d36764485a14b101ef3dffd/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |

### First code: v1 model functions (2026-10-09, evening)
Built in `web/model.js`, one function at a time, each with tests in
`web/model.test.js` (81 tests, all pass: `cd web && node model.test.js`).
Each function was also run with planted bugs to confirm the tests catch them.
- `makeRng(seed)`: seeded random numbers.
- `stepCell`: one year for one cell (hit if rand() < p, fixed order, stops at r).
- `simulatePerson`: N cells, ages 0-84, returns the first age any cell reaches r.
- `simulatePopulation`: M people from one generator, checks inputs. The default
  run (20,000 x 100 cells) takes about 1.5 s.
- `ageGroupRates`: 17 five-year groups, exact person-years.

**Bug found and fixed: the first generator (mulberry32) was biased.** The
default run gave 1,853 cancers when 1,753 were expected (z = 2.5), and 40 more
seeds were also high (z = 3.3). A separate Python simulation matched the
formula, and so did the model with `Math.random`. Over 30 million cells,
mulberry32 gave too few cells with 0 hits (z = -9.6). Each single number was
fine; the problem only showed up across 85 numbers in a row. Switched to sfc32
(all |z| < 2 on the same check). The check is kept in `web/rng-check.js`
(about 10 s). Lesson: passing simple tests on single numbers doesn't prove the
generator is right for this use.

**First graph:** `output/v1-rates.svg` (made by `web/plot-rates.js`). Simulated
rate vs age on log-log axes, with a dashed slope-3 (= r - 1) guide line. From
age 20 up the points follow the line; groups 0-4 and 5-9 have no cases, and
10-19 have 1 each (noise). Hand check: 60-64 = 160 / 97,187 = 164.6 per 100,000.

### Next steps
1. `fitLine` / `logLogFit` (slope and R squared), then `expectedRates` with
   the log1p/expm1 care from the spec, then `zScores` and `runReport`.
2. Add the exact formula's curve to the graph next to the simulation.
EOF

content.text:
All three are done and committed as `1afa512`. Along the way the tests caught a real bug, in the random-number generator.

## 1. `simulatePopulation`, plus `ageGroupRates` for the graph

- **`simulatePopulation`** checks its inputs (bad M, N, r, p and seed all throw an error) and runs everyone from one shared seeded generator. The default run of 20,000 people takes about 1.5 seconds.
- **`ageGroupRates`** computes cases ÷ exact person-years for the 17 age groups. It's tested on your 60–64 picture (cancer at 61 gives 2 person-years) and the edges (ages 0, 64, 65 and 84). Your spec's one-hit check also passes: the rate comes out at 0.0996 and 0.1002 in the first two groups, where we expected p = 0.1.
- **Tests:** all 81 pass. Each new function was also run with planted mistakes, and the tests caught every one.

## The bug the tests caught

The default run gave **1,853 cancers when the formula expects 1,753**. I tracked it down step by step:

| Step | Result |
|---|---|
| 40 more seeds | still too high, z = 3.3, so not bad luck |
| A separate Python simulation | matches the formula, so the formula is right |
| The same model using JavaScript's own `Math.random` | matches the formula, so the model logic is right |
| 30 million single cells with our generator | **too few cells with 0 hits, z = −9.6** |

So the generator I chose, mulberry32, was the problem. Each number on its own looked fine, which is why the earlier tests passed. The flaw only shows up across 85 numbers in a row, and it made about 1.5% too many cancers.

I replaced it with **sfc32**. It passes the same 30-million-cell check (every |z| < 2), and the default run now gives 1,743. That check is saved in `web/rng-check.js` (`node rng-check.js`, about 10 seconds).

## 2. The graph: `output/v1-rates.svg`

Open it in a browser; hovering over a point shows its numbers. It plots the simulated cancer rate against age on log-log axes, with a dashed line of slope 3 = r − 1 for comparison.
- **From age 20 up:** the points follow the slope-3 line, as Armitage & Doll's model predicts.
- **Below age 20:** cases are rare and noisy. Ages 0–9 have no cases, and 10–19 have 1 each.
- **One point to check by hand:** ages 60–64 had 160 cases in 97,187 person-years, which is 164.6 per 100,000 person-years.

## 3. The commit

`1afa512` includes `spec.txt`, the `CLAUDE.md` language change, `web/` (model, tests, slow generator check, graph script), the graph, the progress log and the journal. It hasn't been pushed. Run `! git push` when you're ready.

The course asks for commit messages in your own words, and since this one is mine, you might want to reword it with `! git commit --amend` before pushing.

**A question for you:** the dashed line has slope exactly 3, but the spec says the exact slope at p = 0.005 is 2.84. Looking at the graph, at which end would you expect the points to drift below the line, and why?

content.text:
You're right that the young ages are noisy, but noise isn't what the question is after. There are two different kinds of "off the line":

- **Noise** is random. With only 1 to 20 cases in a group, a point can land above *or* below the line, and a new seed would move it somewhere else. It doesn't change the slope in any one direction.
- **Drift** is systematic. Every seed bends the same way, and that's why the exact formula, which has no randomness at all, gives 2.84 rather than 3.

So the question is where the formula itself pulls away from slope 3. A hint from the tutor session: slope = r − 1 holds only when hits are **rare**, meaning p × age is small.

Work it out for one cell with p = 0.005:
- At age 25, p × age = 0.005 × 25 = ?
- At age 80, p × age = 0.005 × 80 = ?

At which of those ages are hits no longer "rare", so the curve starts to flatten? Bonus: since the dashed line is pinned at the 60–64 point, would the points at that end sit above the line or below it?

content.text:
That's right. At age 80, 0.4 is no longer small, so hits aren't "rare" any more:
- many cells already have 1 or 2 hits;
- the people most likely to get cancer have already had it and dropped out of the risk count.

Both effects slow the rise, so the curve **flattens at old ages**. That gives 2.84 rather than 3.

**The bonus:** the dashed line is pinned at the 60–64 point. A curve that flattens toward old ages sits **below** the slope-3 line past 62.5 and **above** it before 62.5. On the graph, the points from age 25 to 35 do sit a little above the dashed line, as expected. The 70–74 point sits above it too, but that's noise (one seed); the exact formula will show the true shape.

This connects to your scientific question. This flattening comes from saturation, the gradual bend the reviewers measured (slope 4.0 → 2.6 for r = 7, p = 0.05). The lung curve in CI5 drops much faster, from about 8 to about 2. That's why your question tests exposure that **stops** as a stronger cause of the downward bend.

**Next time:**
1. `fitLine` and `logLogFit`, which compute the slope and R² from the points so we don't have to read them off the graph.
2. `expectedRates`, the exact formula, written carefully to avoid the computer-arithmetic problem from the spec.
3. Then add the formula's curve to the graph, so the noise and the drift can be seen separately.
